system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2125-06-20 08:27:00 to 2125-06-23 11:57:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes and chronic back pain was admitted for recurrent nausea and vomiting. She had tried Zofran at home without success and presented with worsening symptoms and back pain. IV antiemetics provided relief, and she tolerated advancement to a regular diabetic diet. Her blood glucose remained stable except for one episode of mild hypoglycemia, managed with food. The insulin regimen was unchanged. Gabapentin was started for back pain as a required trial before lidocaine patch approval. She was advised to use Ativan instead of Zofran for future nausea episodes. She was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up planned with her new care team, including the Chronic Pain Service.
problems: Diabetes with unspecified complication, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled

of precipitants of this. She does carb counting at home, but 
during the hospitalization had several instances of critically 
high readings after consuming ___ ice, etc. without being

was counselled on diabetic diet and evaluated by ___ who

follow up at ___ due to many previously missed appointments 
but should have follow up through ___ after establishing care 
with a PCP. Her insulin supplies were called in to her pharmacy 
on discharge.
.
# Social issues: Patient has been admitted 4 times in the past 
month with multiple previous admissions and has a long history 
of depression/anxiety, non-compliance, and chronic pain. She has 
difficulty keeping outpatient appointments with GI, PCP, 
___, pain clinic, and ___ though social work had been 
trying to establish a multidisciplinary care team for her. On 
this admission, patient expressed the desire to start taking 
care of her health and to try to keep her appointments. She is 
attempting to transition all of her care to ___. She was set up 
with a new PCP on discharge and social work will accompany her 
to this appointment. At that time, they will help set her up 
with the ___ social worker and therapist. She was also given an 
appointment to follow-up with GI. Patient needs intensive 
diabetic management as above, and close follow-up is crucial for 
her. She should continue to follow with social work for ongoing 
support and improved adherence to outpatient appointments, which 
will hopefully reduce her readmission rate.
.
# Anxiety/Psychiatric issues: patient has a long history of 
anxiety, traumatic events, and depression but has not been 
followed as an outpatient. Some of her nausea/vomiting episodes 
were attributed to ""flooding"" and panic attacks in the past. She 
has previously been tried on SSRIs, ativan, and clonidine in 
various combinations but currently only taking ativan as needed 
for anxiety. She did not have active SI/HI on this admission, 
and did not display significant psychiatric symptoms other than 
having mild anxiety and tearfulness on admission. She was 
evaluated by psychiatry for possibly initiating SSRI therapy as 
an inpatient given poor adherence to outpatient follow-up, but 
they thought there was no indication for immediate medical 
therapy as she was not having any active issues. Social work saw 
the patient and will help connect her to the social workers and

.

# HTN: patient takes lisinopril 10mg daily at home, BPs on

# Grade I esophageal varices: found on EGD in ___, she had

She was referred for follow-up with outpatient pain clinic but

.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were brought in this morning for nausea, vomiting, and high blood sugar. Can you tell me what happened?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I ate potato salad and meat last night, and by bedtime I felt nauseous. I had two loose stools. This morning I threw up and my blood sugar was 600 in the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had this before. Were you able to keep anything down after vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, not really. I took Zofran but it didn’t help much. I got scared and called the ambulance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That was the right call. Your blood sugar was very high—627 when you arrived—but you’re not in diabetic ketoacidosis, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not DKA? I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your labs show no acidosis. We gave you IV insulin to bring it down. We also gave Zofran and Dilaudid for nausea and discomfort.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My stomach still feels off, but the pain is better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your exam shows no serious abdominal issues. Lungs are clear, heart normal. We did a chest X-ray to check for infection—it’s fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having a lot of back pain too, since my car accident years ago.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I see you’re on gabapentin and Tylenol. We’ll continue those. No point tenderness in your back, so no new injury.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my diabetes… it’s always so hard to control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk more about that. For now, we’re starting you on fluids and will try to get you on a regular diet later today if you’re stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’ve been doing well—no vomiting, and you kept down some crackers. We’re going to advance you to a regular diabetic diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I was worried I’d throw it up again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor closely. Your blood sugar was high earlier after ice chips—did you know they have sugar in them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I didn’t! I thought it was just water.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a common mistake. We’ll go over diet counseling to help avoid surprises like that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood work came back. Your kidney function was a bit off when you arrived—creatinine 1.2—but it’s improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from my diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it suggests early diabetic nephropathy. But staying hydrated and controlling your sugar helps protect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t know my kidneys were involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s stage I, so very early. But it’s another reason to focus on tight glucose control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying… but my sugars swing so much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed. You had a low sugar this morning—down to 60—after treating a high with too much insulin overnight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just wanted it to come down fast… I get so anxious when it’s high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. That’s actually something we want to talk about—your anxiety and how it affects your symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes the nausea feels like it’s from panic, not my stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry saw you and thinks some episodes may be linked to anxiety ‘flooding,’ but this time, your symptoms may have been from food or high sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So not all of it is in my head?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at all. We did a gastric emptying study yesterday—it was normal. So it’s not gastroparesis this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had that test before and it was normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’re focusing on diabetes control and possible gastroenteritis from the potato salad.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood cultures came back—no infection. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I didn’t have a blood infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Your symptoms weren’t from sepsis. We’re confident it’s related to your diabetes and possibly the food you ate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your A1C result—it’s 12.8%. That means your average sugar has been very high, around 321 mg/dL.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s worse than I thought.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We consulted diabetes management. They recommend keeping your Lantus at 28 units at night, but adjusting how you count carbs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I thought I was doing it right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You are trying, but we’re changing your ratio to 1 unit of Humalog for every 12 grams of carbs—was it 1:10 before?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think so. And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take 1 unit of Humalog for every 40 points your sugar is above 140. We’ll give you a chart to follow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s different. I’ll need to write it down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and keep a log of your finger sticks. It’ll help your new doctor see patterns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve set up a lot for you before discharge tomorrow. You’ll see a new primary care provider in a few days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve missed a lot of appointments before… I feel bad about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We know. That’s why a social worker will go with you to your first visit. They’ll help you connect with a therapist too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That would really help. I want to do better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. You also have a GI follow-up to repeat an endoscopy for your stomach varices and check if H. pylori is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well—no nausea, eating normally, sugars stable. We’re discharging you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. What about my meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue Lantus 28 units at night, Humalog with meals using the new ratio. Gabapentin is now 200 mg three times a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It was 200 mg every 8 hours before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same total dose—just adjusted for easier timing. We’re also adding Zofran as a backup for nausea, but try Ativan first if anxiety is involved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your pharmacy has your insulin and supplies. Keep checking your sugars and write them down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll go to the appointments—I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call if your sugar is very high or low, or if vomiting returns. Otherwise, we’ll see how you do at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and good luck with your new care team.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with type 1 diabetes, chronic back pain, and anxiety was admitted for recurrent nausea, vomiting, and hyperglycemia after eating contaminated food. Her blood glucose was 627 on admission but not in DKA. She improved with IV fluids, insulin, and antiemetics, and tolerated a regular diet without further vomiting. A gastric emptying study was normal, and blood cultures showed no infection. Her A1C was elevated at 12.8%, prompting adjustment of her insulin regimen to 28 units Lantus at bedtime and a revised carb-to-insulin ratio of 1:12 with correction scale of 1 unit Humalog per 40 points above 140. She expressed motivation to improve adherence and was connected with a new primary care provider, social work, and GI follow-up for esophageal varices and H. pylori eradication. She was discharged home in stable condition with updated medications and close outpatient support planned.
